name: Pedro Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good morning, Pedro. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you take me through an ordinary working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy fruit and vegetables for Harbourside Fresh, a family-owned wholesaler that supplies about 200 restaurants and corner groceries. My day starts at four, at the wholesale market, walking the stalls, feeling the tomatoes, shaking hands with growers I've known 15 years. By nine I'm back at the office phoning farms about next week's lettuce and haggling over price. It's early and cold, and I love it, except for the knees.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that a handshake still means something. If a grower says the strawberries will be ready Thursday, they are. What wears me out is the margins, the big supermarkets squeezing everybody, and the paperwork the inspectors want now. I'm 43, my wife Lucia works part-time at our parish school, we've got Mateo and Elena, and a mortgage, and we go to church every Sunday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, good. Same as always. At work I'd tell the younger ones it's a gadget, and that the tomatoes still need someone to pick them. At church or the pub I'd say we've heard this song before with computers. People get excited, then it goes back to normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, that world is fine for me. My job is a handshake and a nose for a good crate, and no program has that. What worries me is the supermarkets, because they could swallow our customers, and the owner, Mr. Marsh, is getting older. If he sells, who knows who runs it. We have two months saved and Lucia's pay is small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I do, rising at four, walking the market. I'd try to bring on a younger buyer to learn from me, because that's how it was done for me. I'd keep saving a bit each month, 100 or so. And I'd tell Mr. Marsh we should go after more small restaurants, where the relationship is worth something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled, mostly. It's the life I know. A little tired, because the hours are long, but I'd say content.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've never used an AI tool. What's your thinking behind that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't use the phone for much except calls. My son Mateo shows me things on it, and he says it can write emails. I'd rather call. When you hear a grower's voice you know if the crop is good or if the grower is covering. A machine can't hear that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets squeezed first if Harbourside has a bad year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mortgage stays, and the church donation stays. We'd cut meals out, the new bike for Elena, and I'd work Saturdays at the market for the extra pay. Lucia would take more hours. It's what you do. You work harder, you don't ask anyone for a handout.

say: It's a **gadget**, and the tomatoes still need someone to pick them.
I'd say we've heard this song before with **computers**.
think: My job is a handshake and a **nose for a crate**, and no program has that.
The **supermarkets** and the owner's age worry me more, with two months saved.
do: Carry on rising at four and bring on a **younger buyer** to learn from me.
Save **100 a month** and push Harbourside toward small restaurants.
feel: **Settled**, a little tired, and content with the life I know.
S0.quote: When you hear a grower's voice you know if the crop is good or if the grower is covering. A machine can't hear that.
fieldNote: Pedro's worries are the **supermarkets** and the owner selling, and he names them without being asked.
He trusts **voices and handshakes**, and keeps his distance from AI.

steps.text: Train a younger buyer at the four o'clock market
Pitch more small restaurant accounts to Mr. Marsh

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, it's not what I'd choose, but it's what's coming, and we should keep our feet on the ground. At work I'd say the office side can change but leave the market side alone. At church I'd say we take care of our people, and companies should too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it worries me. They'd take the ordering, the price lists, the stock checking, which is half my morning. If they take that, I'm the man walking the stalls, and one man walking stalls doesn't make a team of four buyers. I'm average, not special, and I don't know the new tools at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep walking the market, because that's the part that matters. And I'd ask for a few lessons on the new system, quietly, from Mateo. I'd talk to Mr. Marsh about a role for me as the grower-relations man, someone who visits farms. I'd also ask my brother Jorge if his market stall could use me on weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My stomach drops a bit. I've always felt useful, and this says maybe the useful part is getting smaller. That's a hard thing to feel at 43.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your work could a machine take first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The paperwork, the ordering, the price comparisons. I spend two hours a day at a screen, and I hate it anyway. If a machine does the paperwork, fine. What I don't want is for them to say they don't need me at the market too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if buyers were let go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd blame the people at the top who care only about the margin and who never held a crate. And I'd blame the big companies that build these things and don't care who's left. But I wouldn't blame the machine itself. It's just doing what it was built for.

say: The office side can change, but leave the **market side** alone.
At church I'd say we take care of **our people**, and companies should too.
think: They'd take ordering and stock checks, half my morning, leaving **one man** walking the stalls.
I'm **average** and I don't know the new tools at all.
do: Quietly ask my son **Mateo** for lessons on the new system.
Ask Mr. Marsh about a **grower-relations** role and ask my brother about weekend stall work.
feel: **Stomach drops**, because the useful part of my work might shrink.
S1.quote: If a machine does the paperwork, fine. What I don't want is for them to say they don't need me at the market too.
fieldNote: Pedro's fear is about **being useful**, and he separates the screen work he hates from the market work he values.
He blames **bosses and big firms**, not the machine.

steps.text: Ask Mateo to teach me the new ordering system
Ask Mr. Marsh for a grower-relations role visiting farms
Work weekends at my brother's market stall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong that something this big comes in two years and nobody asks the families who'll pay. At work I'd ask for the owner to promise no one gets dropped overnight. I'd vote for whoever promised to protect jobs and keep families together, I don't care for labels.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd lose my job, and I can't see where to go. A computer can read prices, order, and talk to growers by message. I'd be 45 with a mortgage, a bad back and no other trade. We have two months saved. I'd say we have until next summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending, cancel the holiday and the new bike. I'd ask the bank for more time on the mortgage, face to face. I'd go to my brother Jorge, who has the stall, and ask to work for him full time, selling produce directly to people. I'd also ask the parish if there's any work or help, and I'd pray on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fear, plain and heavy. I'd keep it from the kids but I'd be short with people. I'd sit in the truck at five in the morning and not know where to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lucia that evening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, Lucia, I might lose the job within two years. She'd put her hand on mine and say, we'll work it out together. She'd take more hours at the school, and we'd tell the kids to cut back with us. We'd pray, and then do the sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your church friends?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them I'm not sure, honestly. I'd ask them to look after each other if it got hard, because that's what church is. I wouldn't expect a handout, but a hand, yes. Some of them will lose jobs too, and we'd find ways to help.

say: It's **wrong** that something this big comes in two years without asking the families who'll pay.
I'd ask the owner to promise **no one gets dropped** overnight.
think: I think I'd lose my job and **can't see** where to go.
I'd have two months saved and a **bad back**, with until next summer.
do: Cancel the holiday and the **bike**, and ask the bank for more time face to face.
Ask my brother **Jorge** for full-time work at his produce stall.
feel: **Plain, heavy fear**, kept from the kids but showing as short temper.
S2.quote: A computer can read prices, order, and talk to growers by message. I'd be 45 with a mortgage, a bad back and no other trade.
fieldNote: Pedro expects to lose the job and has **no other trade**, which he says unprompted.
His answers turn to **family and parish**, not to new tools or training.

steps.text: Cancel the holiday and the new bike straight away
Ask the bank for more time on the mortgage, in person
Ask Jorge for full-time work at his produce stall
Ask the parish about practical help for families

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's better, but we should still be careful. At work I'd talk to Mr. Marsh about training a younger buyer who can run both sides, the market and the screen. At church I'd tell the young families not to wait for someone to rescue them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, five years is a mercy. I'd be 48 when it arrives, Mateo 18 and Elena 15. I could make Jorge's stall into something real, a proper business selling direct to families and small restaurants. That is hands-on work and it lasts until the robots catch up. I'd have a plan before I'm pushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one I'd take over more of Jorge's Saturday stall and learn his accounts. I'd cut costs, build savings to six months, and pay a bit more on the mortgage. Year two I'd ask Mr. Marsh to let me move into a grower-relations role. And I'd let Mateo teach me enough of the new tools that I don't look foolish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better. It's like getting a reprieve, and I'd feel a bit ashamed that I'd still be thinking of it as a rescue. A man should make his own way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the extra years let you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'm running, with five I'm walking. I'd be able to build the stall slowly, with my own hands. I'd get to know whether people will buy from me, and if they do, I'm halfway there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd want from the government or the company in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want the government to leave businesses alone and make apprenticeships easier. And I'd want Mr. Marsh to be straight with us. If he knows, say so. People can take bad news if they've got time, but not a surprise.

say: Five years is **better**, but we should stay careful and train a younger buyer to run both sides.
I'd tell young families not to wait to be **rescued**.
think: Five years is a **mercy**, and I could make Jorge's stall a real business.
A man should make his **own way**, so I'd feel ashamed to treat it as a rescue.
do: Take over more of Jorge's **Saturday stall** and save six months of expenses.
Ask Mr. Marsh for a **grower-relations** role in year two.
feel: **Relieved**, with a bit of shame at needing the reprieve.
S3.quote: With two years I'm running, with five I'm walking. I'd be able to build the stall slowly, with my own hands.
fieldNote: Pedro uses the time to build a **hands-on stall business**, which suits his values and his trade.
He wants **straight news** from the owner, not a surprise.

steps.text: Take over Jorge's Saturday stall and learn his accounts
Save up to six months of expenses
Ask Mr. Marsh for a grower-relations role in year two
Have Mateo teach me the basic ordering tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a long way off, and we've got time to get ready, so no need to shout about it. At work I'd carry on, and train the next buyers well. At church I'd say good, our kids have time to learn something solid. I'd vote for people who back apprenticeships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, ten years is nearly nothing to fear. I'd be 53, with the mortgage almost paid. If the job went, it would hurt but I'd have a stall or a farm contract to fall back on. I'd worry for Mateo and Elena, more than for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, train the young buyers, and keep working the market. I'd save steadily and pay off the mortgage. I'd probably let Mateo show me some new tools over the years, because if everyone uses them I don't want to be the only man with a pencil. And I'd help Jorge with the stall on weekends, to keep my hand in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Yes. I'd be a bit uneasy reading the news, but at home I'd be fine. I'd say a decade gives a man time to adjust his sails.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does having ten years make you relax?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, but not completely. Ten years has a way of disappearing. My dad said the same thing about the shop closing, and then it closed. So I'd write a date on a calendar, 2032, and check my plan then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Mateo and Elena about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn a trade or a skill with their hands and with people, like cooking, nursing, building, teaching. I'd tell them to be honest and show up, because that's worth more than a title. And I'd tell them to pray, and look after their family.

say: It's a long way off, so **no need to shout** and we can train the next buyers well.
think: At 53 with the mortgage nearly paid, losing the job would **hurt** but not ruin us.
I worry more for **Mateo and Elena** than for myself.
do: Keep working the market, **train young buyers** and pay off the mortgage.
Let Mateo show me new tools and help Jorge at the **stall**.
feel: **Calm** at home, a little uneasy when reading the news.
S4.quote: Ten years has a way of disappearing. My dad said the same thing about the shop closing, and then it closed.
fieldNote: Pedro relaxes only partly, because his **father's shop** closed after similar reassurance.
He tells his kids to learn **hands and people skills**, and to pray and show up.

steps.text: Train the next young buyers at the market
Pay extra on the mortgage each month
Let Mateo show me one new tool each year
Write 2032 on the calendar to check my plan

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Two years to change at my age, with no other trade, is too hard. What would help is time, honest talk from the owner, and a chance to learn something with my hands. And neighbours looking out for each other, which is what the parish does best.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the growers. A lot of them are older than me and they don't even have email. If all the buying goes to machines, who looks after the small farmers? I'd want somebody to.

headlineQuote: If all the buying goes to machines, who looks after the small farmers? I'd want somebody to.
portrait: Pedro is a **43-year-old** produce buyer at a family-owned wholesaler, with a parish-school wife, two kids and a mortgage.
He rises at four, trusts **handshakes** and voices, and has never used AI tools.
He blames **bosses and big firms**, not machines, and wants honest news, apprenticeships and no handouts.
When threatened, he turns to **hands-on work**, his brother's produce stall, family and parish.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture worries him most, with no other trade and only two years.
whatWouldHelp: **Time**, honest talk from the owner, hands-on learning and neighbours looking out for each other.
